A people of the western Pyrenees and the Bay of Biscay, in what is now northern Spain and southwest France, who speak the only surviving pre-Indo-European language of western Europe. The map shows them in 500.

Basque, called Euskara, is not related to any other living language. Genetic studies show the Basques descend largely from the Iron Age people of Iberia, with less later mixing than their neighbours. Roman writers knew a people called the Vascones around Pamplona, and the name Basque comes from theirs.

Rome ruled the area lightly. After Rome fell, the Basques resisted both the Visigoths and the Franks, whose kings campaigned against them again and again. In 778 Basques ambushed the rearguard of Charlemagne's army at the Roncevaux Pass, an event later turned into the Song of Roland. In the 9th century a Basque kingdom formed around Pamplona, later called Navarre.
